title: Corporate Governance, Solvency, and Financial Reporting

questions.stem: Under NIIRA 2025, the minimum proportion of the Board of a Nigerian life insurer that must be Independent Non-Executive Directors is:

opts.x: One-quarter.
One-third.
Half.
Two-thirds.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

NIIRA 2025 and the NAICOM Corporate Governance Guidelines require that at least one-third of the Board of a licensed insurer must be Independent Non-Executive Directors (INEDs). INEDs are directors who: have no material financial relationship with the insurer beyond their director's fees; were not previously employed by the insurer within the past 3 years; are not connected to the insurer's significant shareholders; and exercise independent judgment. This minimum proportion is designed to ensure that the Board has sufficient independent challenge to management.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) One-quarter would be insufficient to ensure genuine independent oversight — a minority this small can be consistently outvoted by executive and non-independent directors.
(C) Half is higher than the NIIRA 2025 minimum — some jurisdictions (e.g., UK corporate governance code) do apply this higher standard, but the Nigerian mandatory minimum is one-third.
(D) Two-thirds would effectively require a Board dominated by INEDs — which is not the NIIRA 2025 standard and would be unusual in most insurance governance frameworks globally.

questions.stem: A Nigerian life insurer's solvency ratio is currently 95%. Under NIIRA 2025's supervisory intervention ladder, this ratio places the insurer in:

opts.x: The Green Zone, requiring no specific NAICOM response.
The Yellow Zone (Threshold), requiring NAICOM formal supervisory review and a capital restoration plan within 30 days.
The Orange Zone (Deficiency), requiring intensive supervision and potentially a NAICOM-appointed special examiner.
The Red Zone (Critical), meaning NAICOM may take control of the company.

questions.answer: (C) The Orange Zone (Deficiency), requiring intensive supervision and potentially a NAICOM-appointed special examiner.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

NIIRA 2025's supervisory intervention ladder has four zones:
• Green Zone: Solvency ratio ≥ 150% — no specific regulatory action required.
• Yellow Zone (Threshold): Solvency ratio 100–149% — NAICOM formal review; capital restoration plan required.
• Orange Zone (Deficiency): Solvency ratio 75–99% — intensive NAICOM supervision; special examiner possible; restrictions on new business writing; dividend ban.
• Red Zone (Critical): Solvency ratio <75% — NAICOM may appoint an administrator or initiate resolution.
At 95%, the insurer is in the Orange Zone — below the minimum solvency ratio of 100% but above the critical threshold.

Note: Specific zone boundaries may vary from the above — candidates should confirm the precise thresholds from the NIIRA 2025 implementing regulations. The question as stated expects (C) based on the Orange Zone description most consistent with a 95% solvency ratio below 100%.

questions.stem: The Contractual Service Margin (CSM) under IFRS 17 represents:

opts.x: The present value of future cash flows expected to be received from policyholders.
The risk adjustment for non-financial risk in the insurance contract measurement.
The deferred profit in an insurance contract at inception, released into income progressively as insurance services are provided.
The minimum capital charge required under the RBC framework for insurance risk.

questions.answer: (C) The deferred profit in an insurance contract at inception, released into income progressively as insurance services are provided.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

Under IFRS 17, when an insurance contract is measured at inception and the fulfilment cash flows (present value of future claims and expenses, less present value of future premiums) produce a net gain, this gain is not recognised as immediate profit — it is deferred as the CSM. The CSM is then released into profit as the insurer provides insurance coverage over the coverage period. The CSM is effectively the insurer's deferred new business profit — it represents the economic value of the insurance services the insurer has committed to provide. A positive CSM indicates profitable new business; a negative CSM (which is an onerous contract loss) is recognised immediately in profit.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) The present value of future cash flows received from policyholders is the premium cash flows component of the fulfilment cash flows — not the CSM itself.
(B) The risk adjustment for non-financial risk is a separate IFRS 17 building block — it compensates the insurer for the uncertainty in non-financial risks (mortality, morbidity, lapses). It is separate from the CSM.
(D) The RBC insurance risk charge (C1 under NIIRA 2025) is a regulatory capital requirement — unrelated to IFRS 17 measurement.

questions.stem: Under NIIRA 2025, a Nigerian life insurer may NOT pay a dividend to shareholders if:

opts.x: The insurer's annual gross written premium income is below a threshold set by NAICOM.
Its solvency ratio is below 100%, or the Statutory Actuary has issued a qualified or adverse actuarial certificate.
The insurer has not obtained a specific NAICOM licence endorsement for dividend payment.
The dividend amount exceeds 50% of the insurer's annual investment income.

questions.answer: (B) Its solvency ratio is below 100%, or the Statutory Actuary has issued a qualified or adverse actuarial certificate.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

NIIRA 2025 imposes two conditions that independently prohibit dividend payment:
1. Solvency ratio below 100%: If the insurer's admissible assets are below its total policy liabilities, paying dividends would further reduce the policyholder-backing assets — directly harming life policyholders. The prohibition protects life fund adequacy.
2. Qualified/adverse actuarial certificate: If the Statutory Actuary is unable to certify that the life fund's policy liabilities are fully covered by admissible assets, the same policy protection rationale applies — dividends cannot be paid when the actuary has raised material solvency concerns.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) There is no GWP threshold for dividend eligibility under NIIRA 2025.
(C) NAICOM does not require a separate licence endorsement for dividend payment — the conditions are solvency-based, not licence-endorsement-based.
(D) A 50% investment income cap on dividends does not exist as a NIIRA 2025 rule — the standard is the solvency ratio and actuarial certificate conditions.

questions.stem: Solvency II's three-pillar structure covers, in order:

opts.x: Capital requirements; corporate governance and risk management; reporting and disclosure.
Actuarial standards; customer conduct; corporate governance.
Premium setting; investment management; reinsurance.
Financial reporting; taxation; regulatory capital.

questions.answer: (A) Capital requirements; corporate governance and risk management; reporting and disclosure.

why.h: Why (A) is Correct

Solvency II's three-pillar structure (which has influenced NIIRA 2025's design) is:
Pillar 1: Quantitative capital requirements — the calculation of technical provisions and the Solvency Capital Requirement (SCR) and Minimum Capital Requirement (MCR) using prescribed models.
Pillar 2: Governance and risk management — the ORSA, the governance requirements (Board composition, risk management function, actuarial function, internal audit), and supervisory review of the insurer's risk management quality.
Pillar 3: Reporting and disclosure — regulatory reporting to the supervisor (RSR) and public disclosure of solvency and financial condition (SFCR).
Why the Others Are Wrong
(B), (C), and (D) describe topics that appear in insurance regulation but are not the Solvency II three-pillar framework description.

questions.stem:
A newly appointed Non-Executive Director of a Nigerian life insurer is a former EFCC investigator who was convicted of accepting a bribe during their government service 8 years ago. The insurer has submitted a fit and proper application to NAICOM for this individual’s appointment.
(a) Explain the two dimensions of the fit and proper assessment (fitness and properness) and identify which dimension is most relevant to this candidate’s background.
(b) Describe how NAICOM would assess this individual’s application and explain the likely outcome.
(c) Explain the consequences for the insurer if it allows this individual to perform Board functions before NAICOM’s assessment is complete.
(d) What ongoing fit and proper obligations does the insurer have once any NAICOM-approved director is in place?

model.h: Part (a) — Fit and Proper: Two Dimensions

Fitness (Professional Competence):
Fitness refers to the individual's professional knowledge, skills, and experience relevant to the role they will perform on the Board. For a NED, fitness requires: an understanding of the insurance industry (or a directly relevant discipline — finance, law, risk management); experience at a senior decision-making level; and the capacity to contribute meaningfully to Board deliberations.

Properness (Personal Integrity and Honesty):
Properness refers to the individual's personal character — specifically, whether they have demonstrated honesty, integrity, and sound judgment in their professional and personal conduct. NAICOM's fit and proper assessment reviews: criminal convictions; regulatory sanctions; disciplinary proceedings; adverse court findings; and any history of dishonest conduct.

Most relevant dimension for this candidate: Properness is the directly relevant dimension. A criminal conviction for accepting a bribe — a fundamental integrity violation — goes to the heart of the properness assessment. The conviction is not historical background noise; it is a definitive finding by a court that this individual engaged in dishonest conduct during a public trust role. This is the most serious category of propriety concern in any financial regulator's fit and proper framework.
Part (b) — NAICOM's Assessment and Likely Outcome

NAICOM's assessment process:
1. Criminal records check: NAICOM will request a certified criminal records check confirming the conviction details — charge, conviction, sentence, and current status (served, on licence, pardoned).
2. EFCC records check: Given the candidate's background as a former EFCC officer, NAICOM will review EFCC's own disciplinary records.
3. Assessment panel review: NAICOM's Supervisory Review team will consider: the nature and gravity of the offence (accepting a bribe is a breach of public trust — directly analogous to the trust obligation of a financial services director); the time elapsed since the conviction (8 years); whether the candidate has demonstrated rehabilitation.

Likely outcome: A conviction for bribery — a corruption offence — will very likely result in a NAICOM refusal of the fit and proper application. The IAIS Insurance Core Principles and NAICOM's own guidance make clear that criminal convictions for offences involving dishonesty create a strong presumption of unsuitability for senior roles in regulated financial institutions. Eight years post-conviction, without clear evidence of rehabilitation and without the offence being spent under any applicable amnesty, the conviction would typically preclude approval.
Part (c) — Consequences of Allowing Board Functions Before NAICOM Approval

NIIRA 2025 requires NAICOM approval before any director or key function holder commences duties. Allowing this individual to perform Board functions before receiving NAICOM's determination:

1. Makes the insurer in breach of NIIRA 2025's fit and proper requirement — a market conduct violation.
2. Exposes the insurer to financial penalty from NAICOM for each day the non-approved individual performs Board functions.
3. Any Board decisions taken with the participation of the non-approved director may be challenged as having been made without a properly constituted Board — creating legal risk for those decisions.
4. If NAICOM subsequently refuses the application and discovers the individual has been performing Board functions in the interim, the regulatory consequences will be significantly more severe — NAICOM may treat this as a deliberate circumvention of the approval requirement.
Part (d) — Ongoing Fit and Proper Obligations

Once a director is NAICOM-approved, the insurer has ongoing obligations:

1. Self-declaration obligation: The director must promptly disclose to the insurer (and the insurer to NAICOM) any subsequent events that affect their fit and proper status — new criminal charges, regulatory investigations, civil judgements, personal insolvency.

2. Annual Board review: The Nomination/Governance Committee must annually review each director's continuing fitness and propriety — confirming that nothing has changed since their last approval.

3. Training and development: The insurer must ensure that all directors maintain the professional competence required for their role — including through induction training, ongoing CPD, and access to relevant information.

4. Immediate notification to NAICOM: If the insurer becomes aware of any information that would affect a director's fit and proper status — for example, a conviction for a financial crime — it must notify NAICOM immediately and suspend the director from Board functions pending NAICOM's assessment of the new information.

questions.stem:
A Nigerian life insurer has the following financial data at its year-end: Total Available Capital ₦32bn; Insurance Risk Charge (C1) ₦15bn; Market Risk Charge (C2) ₦10bn; Credit Risk Charge (C3) ₦5bn; Operational Risk Charge (C4) ₦3bn. The diversification adjustment reduces the Total Risk Charge by 15% from the arithmetic sum.
(a) Calculate the Total Risk Charge (with diversification adjustment).
(b) Calculate the solvency ratio and determine where the insurer sits on the NIIRA 2025 supervisory intervention ladder.
(c) Describe the specific supervisory obligations NAICOM will apply at this solvency ratio level.
(d) If the insurer proposes to pay a dividend of ₦5bn to shareholders, explain whether NAICOM approval is required and whether the payment would be permitted.

model.h: Part (a) — Total Risk Charge Calculation

Arithmetic sum of risk charges:
C1 (Insurance Risk): ₦15bn
C2 (Market Risk): ₦10bn
C3 (Credit Risk): ₦5bn
C4 (Operational Risk): ₦3bn
Arithmetic sum: ₦33bn

Diversification adjustment (15% reduction):
₦33bn × (1 − 0.15) = ₦33bn × 0.85 = ₦28.05bn

Total Risk Charge (with diversification adjustment): ₦28.05bn
Part (b) — Solvency Ratio and Supervisory Intervention Zone

Solvency ratio = Available Capital ÷ Total Risk Charge × 100%
= ₦32bn ÷ ₦28.05bn × 100%
= 114%

Supervisory intervention zone: At 114%, the insurer is in the Yellow Zone (Threshold) — above the minimum solvency ratio of 100% but below the Green Zone threshold (typically 150% in most frameworks). The insurer is technically solvent but is not in the comfortable buffer zone that NAICOM expects well-managed life insurers to maintain.
Part (c) — NAICOM Supervisory Obligations at This Level

In the Yellow Zone at 114% solvency ratio, NAICOM's standard supervisory obligations include:

1. Enhanced reporting: The insurer must submit quarterly (not annual) capital adequacy reports to NAICOM — providing more frequent solvency visibility.

2. Capital restoration plan: If the ratio has declined (e.g., from 130% to 114%), NAICOM will require the insurer to submit a capital restoration plan explaining: the cause of the decline; the actions being taken to restore the ratio to above the Green Zone threshold; and the timeline for achieving this.

3. Heightened supervisory attention: NAICOM's supervisory review team will monitor this insurer more closely — including potentially unannounced desk reviews of financial data and a more frequent supervisory engagement meeting with management.

4. Restrictions on capital distributions: While above 100%, the insurer is in a zone where NAICOM's approval for any capital distribution (dividends) is effectively required (see Part (d)).
Part (d) — Proposed ₦5bn Dividend: Permitted or Not?

Current position post-dividend payment:
Available Capital after dividend: ₦32bn − ₦5bn = ₦27bn
New solvency ratio: ₦27bn ÷ ₦28.05bn = 96% — below the 100% minimum solvency requirement.

Conclusion: The proposed ₦5bn dividend payment is NOT permitted under NIIRA 2025.

The payment would push the solvency ratio below 100% — which is both: (a) prohibited by NIIRA 2025's dividend restriction provision (no dividends if solvency ratio is below 100%); and (b) operationally irrational (it would move the insurer from Yellow Zone to Orange Zone, triggering intensive NAICOM supervision).

Additional consideration: Even at the current 114% level (before dividend), NAICOM would expect to be consulted before any dividend distribution — the Yellow Zone is not a zone of comfortable normalcy. Any dividend in the Yellow Zone requires a Board resolution confirming the insurer's capital adequacy after payment, and NAICOM notification.

questions.stem:
A Nigerian life insurer is implementing IFRS 17 for the first time. Its in-force portfolio includes: 15-year participating endowments; annual renewable group life schemes; and individual term assurance.
(a) Identify which IFRS 17 measurement model (GMM/BBA, PAA, or VFA) applies to each product type and explain your reasoning.
(b) Describe the three building blocks of the GMM and explain the actuarial input required for each.
(c) Explain what the CSM represents for the participating endowment portfolio and describe what a declining CSM would indicate.
(d) Describe two key operational challenges the insurer will face in implementing IFRS 17.

model.h: Part (a) — IFRS 17 Measurement Model by Product Type

rows: Variable Fee Approach (VFA). The VFA applies to contracts with direct participation features — where policyholders share in a pool of underlying items (the with-profit fund's investment returns and surplus). Participating endowments, where the insurer credits reversionary bonuses based on the fund's investment performance, are the archetypal VFA contracts. The insurer's 'fee' for providing coverage is variable — linked to the underlying investment returns.

Premium Allocation Approach (PAA). The PAA applies to short-duration contracts (coverage period ≤ 12 months, or where the PAA produces a measurement not materially different from the GMM). Annual renewable group life schemes have a 12-month coverage period and are renewed annually — the PAA is both eligible and appropriate, simplifying the measurement significantly.

General Measurement Model (GMM / Building Block Approach). For a fixed-premium, fixed-benefit term assurance that does not involve participation in underlying items, the standard GMM applies. The GMM requires the full three building block calculation of fulfilment cash flows (FCF) plus the contractual service margin (CSM).

model.h: Part (b) — Three Building Blocks of the GMM

Building Block 1 — Present Value of Future Cash Flows (PVFCF):
The present value of all expected future cash flows — both outflows (claims, expenses, commissions) and inflows (premiums) — discounted at a current market-consistent risk-free rate (adjusted for any liquidity premium specific to insurance liabilities). Actuarial input required: mortality rates (from EFU or company experience tables); lapse/persistency assumptions; expense assumptions (per-policy and as percentage of premium); investment return assumptions for participating products.

Building Block 2 — Risk Adjustment for Non-Financial Risk (RA):
A compensation for the uncertainty inherent in the amount and timing of non-financial risks (mortality, morbidity, lapse). IFRS 17 does not specify the method for calculating the RA — the insurer chooses a technique (confidence interval; cost of capital; conditional tail expectation) and must disclose the confidence level. Actuarial input required: volatility of mortality experience; correlation between lapse and economic conditions; tail risk scenarios.

Building Block 3 — Contractual Service Margin (CSM):
The deferred profit at inception (see Part (c)). Subsequent CSM movements include: CSM accretion (interest on the opening CSM balance); release to profit over the coverage period (amortised as insurance revenue); and adjustments for changes in assumptions about future services. Actuarial input required: coverage units (the basis for CSM amortisation — for term assurance, coverage units are typically the sum assured in force each period).
Part (c) — CSM for Participating Endowments and a Declining CSM

CSM for participating endowments: Under the VFA, the CSM represents the insurer's net contractual profit from the business of managing the underlying items (the with-profit fund) on behalf of policyholders, over and above a market rate of return. It is the deferred new business profit that the insurer will earn progressively as it provides asset management and insurance services over the 15-year policy term.

A positive CSM at inception confirms that new participating endowment business is economically profitable — the present value of the insurer's fees (variable fee on the fund) exceeds the present value of the insurance services the insurer has committed to provide.

What a declining CSM indicates: The CSM is released (amortised) to profit each period as the insurer provides coverage — so a declining CSM over time is expected. However, a CSM that declines faster than expected — or becomes negative (an onerous contract liability) — indicates:
1. Investment returns are lower than assumed — the variable fee is smaller than expected.
2. Lapses are lower than assumed — the insurer must provide coverage for longer than priced.
3. Mortality is worse than assumed — higher-than-expected claims are eroding the profit margin.
4. Expenses have escalated — the insurer is spending more to service the contract than assumed.
A declining CSM is an early warning signal that management should investigate the cause before it becomes a loss.
Part (d) — Two Key Operational Challenges

1. Granular policy-level data requirements: IFRS 17 requires the measurement of insurance contracts at the group (cohort) level — contracts with similar risk profiles and issued within the same annual cohort. This requires the insurer to have complete, accurate, policy-level data stretching back to the inception of all in-force contracts. Nigerian life insurers with legacy paper-based systems, incomplete electronic records, or multiple migrated policy administration systems may not have the data integrity required for IFRS 17 implementation without a data cleansing exercise costing ₦500m–₦2bn.

2. Integration of finance and actuarial functions: IFRS 17 requires the actuarial model (which calculates fulfilment cash flows, risk adjustments, and CSM movements) to be integrated with the financial reporting system (which produces the income statement and balance sheet). This integration requires: shared data flows; reconciliation frameworks; and a common understanding of IFRS 17 concepts by both the finance team (who produce the P&L) and the actuarial team (who calculate the liability). Most Nigerian life insurers have operated with these functions in separate organisational silos — the integration required for IFRS 17 is a significant people, process, and system challenge.

questions.stem: NIIRA 2025 has fundamentally elevated the corporate governance obligations of Nigerian life insurers, including Board composition requirements, fit and proper assessments, mandatory Board committees, IFRS 17 reporting, and an expanded regulatory return framework. Critically evaluate whether these governance reforms are sufficient to prevent the governance failures — concealed solvency deterioration, misrepresented reserves, management fraud — that have historically damaged policyholder trust in the Nigerian insurance sector. In your answer, discuss: the governance failures that the NIIRA 2025 framework specifically targets; the adequacy of NAICOM’s supervisory powers and enforcement capacity to identify and act on governance failures in a timely manner; the role of the Statutory Actuary and the Board Audit Committee as internal governance mechanisms; and the cultural and leadership conditions required to make the formal governance architecture effective in practice.

model.h: Thesis

NIIRA 2025's governance reforms address the most visible mechanisms of historical governance failures — inadequate Board independence, absent actuarial oversight, opaque financial reporting. But the history of corporate governance failure globally demonstrates that formal governance architecture is necessary but not sufficient. Governance failures occur most dangerously inside technically compliant frameworks, not in their absence.
Governance Failures NIIRA 2025 Specifically Targets

1. Inadequate Board independence: Historical insurer failures in Nigeria often involved Boards dominated by executives and founding shareholders — with no independent check on management's investment, reserving, or disclosure decisions. The mandatory INED requirement (one-third minimum) and the fit and proper regime address this directly.

2. Concealed solvency deterioration: Several historical Nigerian insurer failures involved management reporting solvency ratios that significantly overstated actual solvency — through inadequate reserving, inadmissible asset inclusion, or related-party investment inflation. NIIRA 2025's IFRS 17 requirement (more transparent liability measurement), RBC framework (more risk-sensitive capital calculation), and Statutory Actuary's reporting obligation (direct NAICOM access) all reduce the opportunities for concealment.

3. Management fraud and related-party transactions: The investment of life fund assets in related-party companies or controlled entities at inflated prices was a documented mechanism in historical insurer failures. NIIRA 2025's ALCO requirement, investment policy statement obligation, and concentration limits on related-party investments are directly responsive.
Adequacy of NAICOM's Supervisory Powers

NIIRA 2025 has significantly expanded NAICOM's supervisory powers: on-site inspection rights; financial penalty powers; fit and proper disqualification; special examiner appointment; and resolution powers. These are the right tools.

The adequacy constraint is not the tools — it is the capacity and speed of deployment:
1. NAICOM's inspection team is small relative to 50+ licensed life insurers. Comprehensive on-site inspection of every insurer every year is not feasible.
2. Off-site supervision requires high-quality regulatory data. NAICOM's improved data collection framework (quarterly returns; IFRS 17 disclosures; Statutory Actuary's reports) will improve early warning capability — but only if the data is accurate, which brings us back to the governance culture challenge.
3. NAICOM's enforcement has historically been slow. Governance failures that are detected but not acted on within months embolden those who exploit the regulatory gap.
Role of the Statutory Actuary and Board Audit Committee

The Statutory Actuary is NIIRA 2025's most important internal governance mechanism:
• Annual valuation certification — if the SA refuses to certify the adequacy of reserves, the insurer cannot report a clean solvency position to NAICOM.
• Direct NAICOM access — if management does not address a material concern, the SA must report directly to NAICOM.

The effectiveness of this mechanism depends entirely on the SA's professional independence and courage. An SA who is a full-time employee of the insurer, dependent on management's goodwill for their continued engagement, may face significant personal pressure to approve management's preferred reserving approach. The Institute of Actuaries of Nigeria (IAN) must cultivate a professional culture in which SA independence is a non-negotiable professional standard.

The Board Audit Committee's role: Reviewing the SA's report; questioning management on any areas of actuarial concern; and ensuring the external auditor's coverage extends to the adequacy of insurance liabilities. An effective Audit Committee requires INEDs with financial expertise who can read and challenge actuarial outputs.
Cultural and Leadership Conditions Required

The governance architecture of NIIRA 2025 creates the conditions for accountability — but culture determines whether accountability is exercised:

1. CEO tone at the top: A CEO who treats governance as a compliance overhead creates an organisation where governance failures are covered up rather than surfaced. A CEO who treats good governance as a competitive advantage creates an organisation where risks are disclosed and managed.

2. Whistleblower protection: Nigerian corporate culture has historically punished internal disclosure of concerns. NIIRA 2025's governance improvements will only function if staff who identify governance concerns have a protected, accessible mechanism to raise them — without career consequences.

3. NAICOM's own culture: NAICOM's supervisory effectiveness depends on its own institutional culture — whether inspectors and supervisors are supported in pursuing enforcement actions against well-connected operators, or whether supervisory discretion is influenced by relationships and political considerations. This is the dimension of governance reform that legislation cannot address.

questions.stem: ‘IFRS 17 is not merely a new accounting standard — it is a governance transformation that changes the information available to Boards, management, investors, and regulators about the true financial health of a life insurance company. Its full implementation will require Nigerian life insurers to invest in data governance, actuarial modelling, systems, and the integration of finance and actuarial functions in ways that go far beyond technical accounting compliance.’ Critically evaluate this proposition. In your answer, discuss: the specific governance and management information improvements that IFRS 17 provides relative to IFRS 4 (particularly the CSM as a measure of new business profitability); the operational transformation required to implement IFRS 17 in a Nigerian life insurer with legacy data, systems, and actuarial infrastructure; the challenges of implementing IFRS 17 simultaneously with NIIRA 2025’s other governance reforms (RBC, ORSA, ALCO); and the implications for smaller Nigerian life insurers that lack the resources to implement IFRS 17 independently.

model.h: Thesis

The proposition is correct: IFRS 17 is a governance transformation of the first order. Under IFRS 4 (the replaced standard), insurance contract liabilities could be measured using historical accounting conventions that bore little relationship to economic reality — enabling management to report solvency positions that misrepresented the true financial health of the insurer. IFRS 17's measurement requirements change what information exists, not just how it is presented.
Governance and Management Information Improvements vs IFRS 4

1. The CSM as a new business profitability signal: Under IFRS 4, new business profit was reported in the year of sale — regardless of whether the product was genuinely profitable over its lifetime. This created an incentive to write volume at inadequate prices, reporting apparent profitability that would unwind in future years as claims deteriorated. Under IFRS 17, the CSM defers new business profit to the coverage period — a product that is uneconomically priced has a negligible or negative CSM, immediately visible on the balance sheet. Management cannot hide inadequate pricing behind first-year accounting profit.

2. Risk adjustment disclosure: IFRS 17 requires the explicit quantification and disclosure of the risk adjustment for non-financial risk — the insurer's compensation for mortality, morbidity, and lapse uncertainty. This makes the assumptions underlying the liability measurement visible to investors, auditors, and regulators in a way that IFRS 4's opaque reserving practices did not.

3. Onerous contract identification: Under IFRS 17, contracts that are expected to generate losses (negative CSM) are immediately identified and the full expected loss is recognised at inception. Under IFRS 4, loss-making contracts could be obscured within a profitable portfolio through aggregation.
Operational Transformation Required

1. Data architecture: IFRS 17 requires policy-level data at a granularity that most Nigerian life insurers' legacy systems cannot currently produce. A major data migration and governance programme is required before IFRS 17 can be implemented — typically 12–24 months of intensive data engineering.

2. Actuarial modelling uplift: The fulfilment cash flow calculation requires actuarial models that can project expected future cash flows by product, cohort, and scenario — a level of modelling sophistication beyond what is required for the traditional prospective reserve calculation. Investment in actuarial software (Prophet, Moses, or equivalent) and actuarial talent is required.

3. Finance-actuarial integration: The IFRS 17 close process requires the actuarial calculations (liability measurement, CSM movements) to feed directly into the financial reporting system on a monthly or quarterly basis. This requires system integration, documented data flows, and reconciliation frameworks that do not currently exist in most Nigerian life insurers.

4. Board education: IFRS 17 numbers look different from IFRS 4 — revenue is lower (no more day-1 premium recognition); profit patterns change; the CSM is a new balance sheet item. Boards must understand the new financial narrative well enough to oversee management performance and challenge management's IFRS 17 reporting.
Challenges of Simultaneous Implementation with NIIRA 2025 Reforms

Nigerian life insurers face a governance reform tidal wave: IFRS 17; NIIRA 2025's RBC framework; the mandatory ORSA; the new ALCO requirement; revised regulatory returns — all simultaneously.

Key conflicts:
1. Actuarial talent overload: The Statutory Actuary must simultaneously deliver: the IFRS 17 liability calculation; the NIIRA 2025 RBC calculation; the ORSA stress scenario modelling; and the annual actuarial valuation. Most Nigerian life insurers do not have enough actuarial resources to execute all four competently simultaneously.

2. Data infrastructure competition: Both IFRS 17 (policy-level data) and ORSA (exposure data for stress testing) require investment in the same underlying data infrastructure. Sequencing these investments — IFRS 17 data first, then ORSA data — may be the pragmatic approach, but creates a period during which ORSA quality is limited by data inadequacy.

3. Board attention bandwidth: A Board that is simultaneously navigating RBC capital compliance; IFRS 17 transition; ORSA approval; fit and proper obligations; and mandatory committee establishment is at risk of governance fatigue — where the form of governance is maintained while the quality of governance oversight diminishes.
Implications for Smaller Nigerian Life Insurers

For smaller life insurers (typically those with ₦10–₦20bn total assets), IFRS 17 implementation is an existential capability challenge:

1. Implementation cost: External consulting fees for IFRS 17 implementation range from ₦200m to ₦1bn for medium-sized insurers — a very significant proportion of a smaller insurer's annual profit.

2. Proportionality: The IASB designed a 'simplified approach' (PAA) specifically to reduce the implementation burden for simpler, shorter-duration contracts — which is some relief for group life-focused smaller insurers. But even the PAA requires significant data governance improvement.

3. Talent dependency: Smaller insurers must rely on external consultants rather than internal actuarial capability — creating ongoing cost and dependency rather than building internal capability.

4. Consolidation signal: IFRS 17's implementation burden is one more factor pushing smaller insurers toward consolidation — whether to merge with larger entities that have the scale to absorb IFRS 17 implementation cost, or to partner with other insurers to share actuarial and technology infrastructure.
